classification_method: Direct DeepSeek API reason-level semantic classification using official Retraction Watch reason definitions, fixed label set, JSON output, temperature=0, top_p=1, thinking disabled, and validation checks.

research_content_reliability.label: Research-content reliability
research_content_reliability.definition: Signals that the reliability, reproducibility, validity, or evidentiary integrity of the research content itself is questioned.
include: computer/AI-generated article content when it affects content authenticity
paper-mill or fabricated article production when it indicates article-level reliability risk
exclude: journal/publisher procedural acts without a content reliability signal
research_content_reliability.manuscript_link: Supports discussion of the reliability of the published product/scientific record, without assigning fault.

attribution_authorship_disclosure_integr.label: Attribution, authorship, and disclosure integrity
attribution_authorship_disclosure_integr.definition: Signals concerning who created, approved, owned, disclosed, cited, or was credited for the work, including attribution and disclosure problems.
exclude: generic data/image/results unreliability without attribution/authorship/disclosure element
attribution_authorship_disclosure_integr.manuscript_link: Matches the manuscript's concern with transparent relationships among authors, editors, reviewers, and publishers and with disclosure/attribution integrity.

editorial_peer_review_governance.label: Editorial and peer-review governance
editorial_peer_review_governance.definition: Signals that editorial decision-making, peer review, journal/publisher procedures, or editorial independence/governance mechanisms are implicated.
include: publication-policy breach or sanction when it concerns publication governance
exclude: journal/publisher investigation as source only unless the reason itself concerns editorial/peer-review procedure
content unreliability without editorial or peer-review process signal
editorial_peer_review_governance.manuscript_link: Directly supports the manuscript's themes of peer-review integrity, editorial independence, proportionality, and governance.

post_publication_transparency_due_proces.label: Post-publication transparency, due process, and oversight
post_publication_transparency_due_proces.definition: Signals concerning post-publication investigation, notice transparency, correction/retraction status, availability/removal, procedural communication, institutional/legal oversight, or appeal/objection-related process.
include: notice lacks information or is inaccessible
exclude: data/image/results problems without post-publication process information
peer-review compromise as pre-publication process unless linked to post-publication oversight
attribution/authorship issues without procedural transparency/oversight component
post_publication_transparency_due_proces.manuscript_link: Matches the manuscript's core language on transparency, clear reasons, proportionality, due process, appeal, and publisher/journal oversight.

items.definition_used: The corresponding author(s) did not respond to journal/publisher requests for response, clarification, etc., about one or more concerns/issues with a publication. RW does not apply this reason when the lack of response is only to the language or posting of a notice of correction/EOC/retraction.ion after prior contact by Journal, Publisher or other original Authors
items.caution: The reason describes a procedural failure (non-response) rather than a direct content or integrity issue. It is a status/transparency signal, not a primary cause of retraction. Main figure recommendation is false because the category is only broadly supported and the reason is secondary to underlying concerns.
items.semantic_rationale: Author unresponsiveness impedes post-publication clarification and due process, fitting the oversight category broadly. It does not directly indicate content unreliability, authorship issues, or editorial governance failures.

items.raw_reason: Bias Issues or Lack of Balance
items.canonical_reason: Bias Issues or Lack of Balance
items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about balance or bias in any of the methods, analyses, results or any part of the published content. RW entries using this reason do not state or imply, nor should users infer, any intentionality.
items.caution: The definition covers methods, analyses, results, or any part of published content, so problem_object is broad. Process_signal and actor_context are inferred from typical investigation sources, not explicitly stated. No intentionality is implied.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition directly addresses questions about balance or bias in research content, which falls under research_content_reliability. Other categories are not supported because the definition does not mention authorship, editorial processes, or post-publication transparency.

items.definition_used: A journal/publisher/institution states that one or more authors violated one or more of the journal/publisher/institution’s policy(ies). RW will use this reason when no other information about the correction/EOC/retraction is available (i.e., the notice only states that there was a breach of policy), or when the breach of policy (as an additional reason) cannot be addressed by existing reasons.
items.caution: The definition is intentionally broad and used when no specific policy breach details are available. It signals a policy violation by an author but does not specify which policy, making it a transparency/oversight signal rather than a direct indicator of research content or authorship integrity issues.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a notice stating an author violated a policy, which is a post-publication transparency signal about a policy breach. It does not inherently indicate problems with research content, authorship, or peer review, but rather a general policy violation. Therefore, it maps to post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight as a broad oversight category.

items.definition_used: Retracted content is used in citations or referencing.
items.caution: The reason indicates reliance on retracted work, which may affect the integrity of the citing manuscript's references. It does not necessarily imply the citing authors were aware of the retraction at the time of citation.
items.semantic_rationale: Citing retracted work involves references/attribution and raises concerns about the reliability of the manuscript's scholarly foundation, fitting attribution integrity and post-publication transparency categories.

items.definition_used: Civil legal proceedings were instigated in response to the article and/or notice(s), or civil legal proceedings resulted in the correction/EOC/retraction/etc.
items.caution: The reason describes a legal process external to the manuscript's content, not a direct integrity issue. It is a status/process signal, not a primary cause.
items.semantic_rationale: Civil proceedings are a legal process triggered by the article, indicating post-publication oversight and transparency, but not directly implicating research content, authorship, or editorial governance.

items.definition_used: Complaints about one or more authors in addition to concerns about the original article. RW may also use this reason for cases in which something about one or more authors is called into question following any notice, i.e., when complaints escalate to being entirely author-based.
items.caution: The definition focuses on complaints about authors, which may involve various underlying issues. The assigned categories reflect the author-centric nature, but specific problems (e.g., data, ethics) are not explicit in the definition.
items.semantic_rationale: The reason centers on complaints about authors, directly implicating authorship and attribution integrity. The definition mentions concerns about the original article, but the escalation to author-based complaints supports attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity as the primary category.

items.definition_used: Complaints about one or more companies/institutions in addition to concerns about the original article. RW may also use this reason for cases in which something about one or more companies/institutions is called into question following any notice, i.e., when complaints escalate to being entirely company/institution-based.
items.caution: The reason focuses on complaints about companies/institutions, which may relate to post-publication oversight but does not directly assert issues with research content, authorship, or editorial processes. It is a status/notice signal about external concerns, not a substantive manuscript integrity category.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes complaints about companies/institutions, which can involve investigations or concerns raised after publication, aligning with post-publication transparency and due process oversight. However, it does not inherently indicate problems with research content, authorship, or editorial governance, so only the oversight category is assigned broadly.

items.definition_used: Complaints about one or more third parties in addition to concerns about the original article. RW may also use this reason for cases in which something about one or more third parties is called into question following any notice, ie., when complaints escalate to being entirely third party-based.
items.caution: The reason is a metadata signal about complaints involving third parties, not a direct indicator of manuscript content or process flaws. It primarily reflects post-publication transparency and due process oversight, but lacks specificity for main-figure prevalence.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes complaints about third parties in relation to an article, which falls under post-publication transparency and due process oversight as it involves external scrutiny and potential notice opacity. No direct evidence of research content, authorship, or editorial process issues is implied.

items.definition_used: The peer review was not performed in accordance with the journal’s guidelines or ethical standards
items.semantic_rationale: The definition directly describes a failure in the peer review process, which maps to editorial_peer_review_governance. No other categories are supported.

items.definition_used: Contains any content that was created via a text generator, randomizing algorithm, generative AI, etc. Some examples of these tools include Mathgen, Scigen, ChatGPT.
items.caution: Content-authenticity/reliability signal only for the principal analysis; do not infer authorship or disclosure failure without an explicit co-label.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes content created by AI or algorithms, which can affect the reliability of research content (e.g., fabricated data, methods, or conclusions) and may involve undisclosed authorship or attribution issues. The process signal is ai_computer_content, and the actor context is author as the typical source of such content.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about any non-human test or study subject(s).
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: Animal welfare concerns directly implicate ethical treatment of subjects, which can affect the reliability of research content and reflect on author compliance with ethical standards, thus supporting research_content_reliability and attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity categories.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about published content, or undefined sections of it.
items.caution: The definition is too broad and non-specific to assign any manuscript-facing category reliably. It functions as a catch-all notice of unresolved concerns without indicating whether the issue pertains to research content, authorship, editorial processes, or post-publication oversight.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a general notice of controversy or dispute about published content without specifying the nature of the concern. It lacks the specificity required to map to any of the four manuscript-facing categories, which require more concrete indications of problems with research reliability, attribution, editorial governance, or post-publication processes.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about authorship and/or affiliation, except for false/forged authorship or false/forged affiliation. False/forged authorship or false/forged affiliation are covered under their own reasons.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly covers disputes about authorship/affiliation, directly aligning with the attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity category.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about any of the data.
items.caution: The definition is broad and does not specify the nature or source of the concern; actor_context is unclear because the definition does not indicate who raised the concern.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition covers any question, controversy, or dispute about data, which directly relates to the reliability of research content.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about any human test or study subject(s).
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition covers any question about human subjects, which directly implicates research ethics and welfare. This can affect the reliability of research content and may involve failures in authorship/disclosure regarding ethical approvals. The process signal is research ethics approval, but the actor context is unclear as the definition does not specify who raised the concern.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about one or more images, or part(s) of one or more images.
items.caution: The definition is broad and does not specify the nature of the concern, so process_signal and actor_context are left empty or unclear. The category research_content_reliability is assigned because image concerns directly relate to the reliability of presented data.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a dispute about images, which are part of research content. This directly implicates the reliability of the research content, supporting the research_content_reliability category.

items.definition_used: Local CSV term not present in extracted Appendix B definitions; treated as concerns/issues about methods by semantic analogy.
items.caution: Definition is not from official Appendix B; assigned by semantic analogy. Actor context is unclear as the source of concerns is not specified.
items.semantic_rationale: Concerns about methods directly relate to the reliability of research content, as methods underpin the validity of results and conclusions.

items.definition_used: The peer review was not performed solely through journal error, or there are problems with the peer review that are not covered under “Fake Peer Review”.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes problems with peer review not solely due to journal error, directly implicating editorial and peer review governance.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about references, citations, attributions, etc. This could include fabricated/falsified references, reference stacking, citing other work with an EOC or correction, etc.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly targets references, citations, and attributions, which directly maps to the attribution/authorship/disclosure integrity category. The process signal is content reuse/duplication because reference stacking or citing corrected work involves reuse or duplication concerns. Actor context is unclear as the definition does not specify who raised the concern.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about the results and/or conclusions.
items.caution: The reason is broad and does not specify the nature of the concern, so it could overlap with other categories if more details emerge.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition directly targets questions about results/conclusions, which falls under research content reliability. No specific process or actor is indicated, so process_signal is notice_opacity and actor_context is unclear.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about third party involvement.
items.caution: Third-party involvement is too broad for a main mechanism category; retained only as a broad process/oversight audit signal.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition 'Any question, controversy or dispute about third party involvement' does not map to any of the four manuscript-facing categories because it lacks specificity about the content, process, or integrity aspect affected. It is a broad metadata signal about an external party's role in a dispute, not a substantive integrity issue.

items.definition_used: Any question, controversy or dispute about author(s), editor(s), any third party and/or peer reviewer(s) having affiliations with companies, associations or institutions that may serve to influence how they conduct their role in any part of the research and/or publication process(es).
items.caution: Conflict of Interest is a broad integrity concern that can affect multiple stages of research and publication. It is not limited to a single problem object or process, and may involve various actors. The assignment to manuscript categories is based on the potential influence on authorship/disclosure and editorial/peer review governance, but the actual impact may vary.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition encompasses questions about affiliations that may influence conduct in any part of the research or publication process. This directly relates to attribution, authorship, and disclosure integrity (e.g., undisclosed competing interests) and editorial/peer review governance (e.g., compromised objectivity). The problem object is set to article_general as the conflict can affect the entire work, and process signals include editorial_breach and publication_policy_or_sanction due to potential violations of disclosure policies. Actor context includes author, editor, and third party as all may have relevant affiliations.

items.definition_used: Impurities were found or suspected within cell lines or tissues.
items.semantic_rationale: Contamination directly compromises the reliability of research materials (cell lines/tissues), fitting research_content_reliability. The definition implies investigation by various parties, but no specific process or actor is mandated, so process_signal and actor_context are inferred broadly.

items.definition_used: Impurities were found or suspected within compounds, reagents or solutions used in experiments.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: Contamination of materials directly compromises the reliability of experimental results, fitting research_content_reliability. The definition focuses on impurities in experimental compounds, which is a methods/materials problem. Investigation is implied but not specified, so journal/publisher investigation is a reasonable default process signal. Author is the typical actor context as they handle materials.

items.definition_used: Dispute concerning permissions or ownership of materials (equipment, cell lines, etc.), technologies, images, text, patents, etc.
items.caution: Copyright claims can involve ownership disputes that may not directly affect research content reliability; classification is broad because the definition covers a range of materials and permissions, and the impact on manuscript integrity depends on context.
items.semantic_rationale: Copyright claims involve disputes over permissions or ownership of materials, text, images, or data, which directly relates to attribution and disclosure integrity. They also trigger legal processes and post-publication oversight, as journals may need to address rights issues after publication.

items.definition_used: Criminal legal proceedings were instigated in response to the publication and/or notice(s), or criminal legal proceedings resulted in the correction/EOC/retraction/etc.
items.caution: The reason indicates legal proceedings but does not specify whether they relate to research content, authorship, or editorial issues. It is a status/process signal, not a direct indicator of manuscript integrity problems. Main figure recommendation is false because the category assignment is broad and the reason is primarily a transparency/due-process marker.
items.semantic_rationale: Criminal proceedings are a legal process that can lead to post-publication actions like retractions, fitting the post-publication transparency and due process oversight category. The definition does not specify the underlying manuscript issue, so other categories are not directly supported.

items.raw_reason: Date of Article and/or Notice Unknown
items.canonical_reason: Date of Article and/or Notice Unknown
items.definition_used: The article and/or notice do not have clear publication dates. RW may also use this reason when a publisher overwrites the original article’s HTML page with the notice, without changing the publication date to reflect the change.
items.caution: This reason is a metadata transparency signal about missing or overwritten dates, not a direct indicator of research content or authorship issues. It supports post-publication transparency only broadly.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes unclear or overwritten publication dates, which is a notice opacity issue under post-publication transparency, with the journal/publisher as the relevant actor context.

items.definition_used: An attribution made by co-founders of Retraction Watch indicating admirable behavior by one of the involved parties
items.caution: The definition describes a subjective editorial attribution of admirable behavior, not a specific manuscript integrity issue, process, or actor context. It does not map to any of the four manuscript-facing categories.
items.semantic_rationale: The reason is a meta-commentary on behavior, lacking concrete problem objects, process signals, or actor contexts required for manuscript category assignment.

items.raw_reason: Duplication of Content through Error by Journal/Publisher
items.canonical_reason: Duplication of Content through Error by Journal/Publisher
items.definition_used: Duplication of published content due to an error by the journal or publisher.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes duplication of published content caused by a journal/publisher error. This directly involves editorial and production governance (editorial_peer_review_governance) and post-publication correction/transparency processes (post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight). The problem object is the article as a whole, and the process signals are journal error and duplication handling.

items.definition_used: Duplication of any of the data.
items.semantic_rationale: Duplication of data directly concerns the reliability of research content, as it involves the integrity of reported data.

items.definition_used: Duplication of any of the text.
items.caution: Text-only duplication is treated as attribution/publication-integrity metadata, not research-content reliability; data, image, and article-level duplication follow separate object rules.
items.semantic_rationale: Text duplication directly impacts the reliability of the research content (research_content_reliability) and raises concerns about proper attribution and authorship disclosure (attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity). The definition does not specify the nature or extent, so both are applicable.

items.definition_used: Duplication of a published item, or undefined sections of it.
items.caution: Duplication may overlap with plagiarism or self-plagiarism, but the definition is broad and does not specify intent or fault. Actor context is unclear as the definition does not indicate who identified or investigated the duplication.
items.semantic_rationale: Duplication of a published item or sections directly impacts the reliability of research content and raises questions about attribution and disclosure integrity, as it may involve reuse without proper citation or permission.

items.definition_used: Duplication of one or more images, or part(s) of one or more images.
items.semantic_rationale: Image duplication directly concerns the reliability of research content, as it involves potential data manipulation or error in visual evidence.

items.definition_used: Expression of Concern has been removed or is no longer applicable. Not to be confused with an “Upgraded to Retraction”
items.caution: This is a status-only notice about the removal of an Expression of Concern, not about the underlying content. It does not directly indicate a problem with research content, authorship, or editorial processes beyond the transparency of the notice itself.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a change in the status of a post-publication notice (Expression of Concern lifted), which falls under post-publication transparency and due process oversight. It does not inherently signal issues with research content, authorship, or editorial governance, but rather a metadata update about a notice.

items.definition_used: An error attributed to a journal/publisher.
items.caution: The definition is broad; the error could range from production mistakes to editorial process failures. Without specifics, it is unclear if the error directly affects research content reliability or attribution integrity, so those categories are not assigned.
items.semantic_rationale: The error is attributed to the journal/publisher, directly implicating editorial and production processes (editorial_peer_review_governance) and potentially requiring post-publication corrective transparency (post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight). The problem object is the article in general, as the error's scope is unspecified.

items.definition_used: An error attributed to any third party.
items.caution: Third-party error is non-specific; retained only as a broad process/oversight audit signal.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition 'An error attributed to any third party' does not provide enough detail to map to any of the four manuscript-facing categories. It could involve research content, authorship, editorial processes, or post-publication issues, but without further specification, no category is justified.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in the evaluation of any of the data or in any calculation(s).
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes errors in data evaluation or calculations, directly undermining the reliability of research content. This maps strictly to research_content_reliability.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in the choice or identification of any of the cell lines or tissues.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes errors in cell line/tissue choice or identification, which directly undermines the reliability of research materials and thus the research content. This fits the research_content_reliability category strictly.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in any of the data.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly states errors in data, directly impacting research content reliability.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in one or more images, or part(s) of one or more images.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes errors in images, which directly concerns the reliability of research content (data/image integrity). No process or actor is specified, so actor_context is unclear.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in one or more experimental materials. including reagents, mixing bowls, equipment or instrumentation.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes errors in experimental materials (reagents, equipment), which directly affect the reliability of research content. This maps to research_content_reliability. The error is a material mistake, not a process or transparency issue, so other categories are not supported.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in the choice of and/or implementation of experimental protocol(s).
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes errors in experimental protocols, which directly affect the reliability of research content. The problem object is methods/materials, and the process signal is journal/publisher error (as the error is in the published methods). Actor context is author, as authors typically implement protocols.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in any of the results and/or the conclusions.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly states errors in results/conclusions, directly undermining research content reliability.

items.definition_used: One or more errors in any of the text.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: Text errors can affect the reliability of the research content, as they may misrepresent findings or methods. The definition directly points to text issues, which fall under research content reliability.

items.definition_used: When a journal/publisher/institution states that one or more authors have not met the journal/publisher/institution’s standards of publishing and/or research ethics. RW will use this reason when no other information about the correction/EOC/retraction is available (i.e., the notice only states that there was an ethical violation), or when the ethical violation (as an additional reason) cannot be addressed by existing reasons.
items.caution: Generic ethical-violation label used when no more specific reason is available; do not infer content, attribution, or editorial mechanism from this label alone.
items.semantic_rationale: The reason indicates a failure to meet publishing/research ethics standards by authors, as stated by a journal/publisher/institution. This broadly implicates authorship and disclosure integrity (attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity) and the editorial/peer review governance that enforces such standards (editorial_peer_review_governance). The problem object is the article as a whole, and the process involves investigation and policy enforcement by the journal/publisher or institution.

items.definition_used: When a journal/publisher/institution states that one or more company(ies)/institution(s)/thirdparty(ies) have not met the journal/publisher/institution’s standards of publishing and/or research ethics. RW will use this reason when no other information about the correction/EOC/retraction is available (i.e., the notice only states that there was an ethical violation), or when the ethical violation (as an additional reason) cannot be addressed by existing reasons.
items.caution: The definition is broad and often used when details are unavailable; it signals an ethical breach by an entity but does not specify the nature of the problem (e.g., data, authorship). Main figure not recommended because the reason is a catch-all for opaque notices.
items.semantic_rationale: The reason indicates a journal/publisher/institution found a company/institution/third party violated publishing/research ethics standards. This implicates editorial/peer review governance (standards enforcement) and post-publication transparency (notice of ethical breach). The problem object is article_general due to lack of specificity. Process signals include investigations by journal/publisher, institution, or third party, and a publication policy/sanction. Actor contexts are company/institution, third party, and journal/publisher as the investigating body.

items.definition_used: The notice does not clearly state that the authors reused ideas, text, or images from one of their previously published items without suitable citation
items.caution: The definition focuses on opaque notice language about reuse without citation, which implicates both content reliability and attribution integrity. However, the term 'euphemisms' suggests the notice may obscure the nature of duplication, so the exact problem (text, image, data) is inferred broadly.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes reuse of ideas, text, or images without proper citation, directly affecting research content reliability (duplicated content) and attribution/authorship integrity (missing citation). The notice's lack of clarity also signals notice opacity.

items.definition_used: The notice does not explicitly state that the reason for the notice is due to misconduct, despite a journal, publisher, company, institution, government agency or author explicitly stating that there was misconduct.
items.caution: This reason describes a transparency failure in the notice itself, not the underlying content problem. It is a metadata/status signal about how the reason is communicated, not a direct indicator of research content unreliability or authorship/editorial integrity issues. Main figure recommendation is false because the category is about post-publication transparency, which is typically not a main figure prevalence category.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition focuses on a notice that fails to explicitly state misconduct despite an external statement of misconduct. This directly relates to post-publication transparency and due process oversight because the notice's opacity undermines clear communication of the retraction reason. The problem object is the article in general, as the notice concerns the overall retraction communication. Process signal is notice_opacity, and actor contexts include all entities mentioned as potential sources of the misconduct statement.

items.definition_used: The notice describes plagiarism of material without using the words “plagiarize(d)” or “plagiarism.”
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly describes plagiarism of material, which is a form of text reuse without proper attribution, directly mapping to attribution/authorship/disclosure integrity.

items.definition_used: The false/forged use of an affiliation/institutional name in the publication process.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly describes false or forged use of an affiliation, which directly violates authorship and disclosure integrity.

items.definition_used: The false/forged use of one or more author names in the publication process.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly describes false/forged use of author names, directly mapping to authorship integrity concerns.

items.definition_used: Falsification or fabrication of any data in order to mislead.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly describes falsification or fabrication of data to mislead, which directly undermines the truth of research content, fitting research_content_reliability. No other categories are supported.

items.definition_used: Falsification or fabrication in/of one or more images, or part(s) of one or more images, in order to mislead.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly describes manipulation of images to mislead, directly undermining the trustworthiness of research content.

items.definition_used: Falsification or fabrication of results in order to mislead.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly describes falsification or fabrication of results to mislead, directly undermining the trustworthiness of research content.

items.definition_used: The paper was intentionally drafted with fabricated or falsified data or other content with the goal of testing a journal or publisher’s manuscript acceptance policies.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes intentional fabrication/falsification of data or content to test acceptance policies, directly undermining research content reliability and exposing editorial/peer review governance failures.

items.definition_used: When informed/patient consent documentation is deemed insufficient or is not available or the participant later disputes/withdraws their approval.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes insufficient, unavailable, or withdrawn consent, which directly implicates research ethics approval processes and can undermine the ethical foundation of the research content, thereby affecting both attribution/disclosure integrity and content reliability.

items.definition_used: An investigation by the company/institution listed as the affiliation of one or more authors.
items.caution: Investigation source/locus signal only; not actor fault, oversight failure, or substantive cause. Included as post-publication process-source metadata.
items.semantic_rationale: The reason indicates an institutional investigation, which is a process signal, but does not specify what is being investigated (e.g., data, authorship, ethics). Therefore, no manuscript category can be assigned based solely on this definition.

items.definition_used: An investigation by the journal/publisher of the article.
items.caution: Investigation source/locus signal only; not actor fault, oversight failure, or substantive cause. Included as post-publication process-source metadata.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes an investigation by the journal/publisher, which directly maps to post-publication transparency and due process oversight. It does not inherently indicate issues with research content, authorship, or editorial governance, though such issues may be discovered during the investigation.

items.definition_used: An investigation by the United States Office of Research Integrity (ORI).
items.caution: Investigation source/locus signal only; not actor fault, oversight failure, or substantive cause. Included as post-publication process-source metadata.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes an investigation by a government oversight body (ORI) into research integrity. This is a process signal (official_misconduct_process) with actor_context ori_government. No specific problem_object is mentioned, and the definition does not inherently imply a particular manuscript-facing category; it could relate to any of them depending on the investigation's focus. Therefore, no manuscript category is assigned.

items.definition_used: An investigation by any third party that is not the United States Office of Research Integrity (ORI).
items.caution: Investigation source/locus signal only; not actor fault, oversight failure, or substantive cause. Included as post-publication process-source metadata.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes an investigation by a non-ORI third party, which is a process signal (third_party_investigation) with actor context (third_party). It does not inherently indicate a problem with research content, authorship, editorial processes, or post-publication oversight; it merely notes that an investigation occurred. Therefore, no manuscript category is assigned.

items.definition_used: One or more authors did not approve one or more parts of the research or publication process(es). RW also uses this reason if the notice mentions a lack of documentation of alleged approval.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition directly concerns author approval of research or publication processes, which falls under authorship integrity. The problem object is authorship/affiliation and the article as a whole, with the process signal being the authorship/publication process. The actor context is author, as the lack of approval originates from an author.

items.definition_used: One or more companies/institutions did not approve one or more parts of the research or publication process(es). RW also uses this reason if the notice mentions a lack of documentation of alleged approval.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes missing institutional approval for research or publication, which implicates authorship/disclosure integrity (attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity) and governance of the publication process (editorial_peer_review_governance). The problem object is article_general because the lack of approval affects the overall publication, and the process signal is research_ethics_approval_process, with actor_context company_institution.

items.raw_reason: Lack of Approval from Third Party
items.canonical_reason: Lack of Approval from Third Party
items.definition_used: One or more third parties did not approve one or more parts of the research or publication process(es). RW also uses this reason if the notice mentions a lack of documentation of alleged approval.
items.caution: The definition is broad, covering any missing third-party approval for research or publication processes. Without specifics, it could relate to ethics approval, data use agreements, or institutional permissions. The assignment to manuscript categories is based on the likely impact on research integrity and governance, but the exact nature of the missing approval is ambiguous.
items.semantic_rationale: Missing third-party approval directly implicates research ethics approval processes and may indicate notice opacity if documentation is lacking. This affects the integrity of authorship/disclosure and editorial governance, as proper permissions are foundational to ethical publication.

items.raw_reason: Lack of IRB/IACUC Approval and/or Compliance
items.canonical_reason: Lack of IRB/IACUC Approval and/or Compliance
items.definition_used: Failure to obtain consent from the institutional ethical review board overseeing human or animal experimentation prior to initiation of study, or failure to provide proof of such
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes failure to obtain or prove ethical review board approval, which directly concerns research ethics approval process and ethics/welfare of subjects. This impacts both the integrity of authorship disclosures (missing required approvals) and the reliability of research content (non-compliance with ethical standards).

items.definition_used: When a journal/publisher/author/third party uses the phrase “legal reasons,” documents litigation or legal threats, or mentions one or more specific laws
items.caution: Legal reasons are a post-publication transparency signal, not a direct indicator of manuscript content or integrity issues. The definition does not specify what aspect of the article is affected, so problem_object is set to article_general. Actor_context is unclear because the definition mentions multiple possible actors without specifying who invoked the legal reasons.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a notice or process involving legal reasons, litigation, or laws, which aligns with post-publication transparency and due process oversight. It does not directly indicate issues with research content, authorship, or editorial governance, so only the transparency category is assigned.

items.definition_used: Manipulation of any data.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition explicitly states manipulation of data, directly indicating compromised research content reliability.

items.definition_used: Manipulation of one or more images, or part(s) of one or more images.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: Image manipulation directly compromises the reliability of research content, as images are part of the data or results. No process or actor is specified in the definition.

items.definition_used: Manipulation of any results.
items.caution: Definition is broad; no specific process or actor indicated. Assigned to research_content_reliability because manipulation directly undermines result trustworthiness.
items.semantic_rationale: Manipulation of results directly compromises the reliability of research content, fitting the research_content_reliability category. No explicit process or actor is mentioned, so process_signal and actor_context are minimal.

items.definition_used: One or more authors misunderstood one or more parts of a message sent to and/or from one or more authors.
items.caution: Communication-process signal only; not misconduct, fault, or substantive retraction mechanism. Contextual-exclusion sensitivity is required.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition focuses on author misunderstanding during communication, which is a general authorship process issue but lacks specific connection to the defined manuscript categories.

items.definition_used: One or more companies/institutions misunderstood one or more parts of a message sent to and/or from one or more companies/institutions.
items.caution: Communication-process signal only; not misconduct, fault, or substantive retraction mechanism. Contextual-exclusion sensitivity is required.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition refers to a misunderstanding in messages between companies/institutions, which is a general procedural issue without direct link to manuscript reliability, attribution, peer review, or post-publication processes. It is too ambiguous to assign any manuscript-facing category.

items.definition_used: One or more journals/publishers misunderstood one or more parts of a message sent to and/or from one or more journals/publishers.
items.caution: Communication-process signal only; not misconduct, fault, or substantive retraction mechanism. Contextual-exclusion sensitivity is required.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a journal/publisher misunderstanding in communication, which is an editorial process error (editorial_peer_review_governance) and may impact transparency or due process (post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight). No direct evidence of research content problems or attribution issues.

items.definition_used: One or more third parties misunderstood one or more parts of a message sent to and/or from one or more third parties.
items.caution: Communication-process signal only; not misconduct, fault, or substantive retraction mechanism. Contextual-exclusion sensitivity is required.
items.semantic_rationale: The reason describes a misunderstanding in communication by a third party, which is a procedural or transparency notice about an external error, not a reliability, attribution, governance, or oversight issue with the manuscript itself.

items.definition_used: An investigation by an incorporated company, institution or government agency into misconduct allegations (founded or unfounded) and/or the finding(s) of misconduct by an incorporated company, institution or government agency.
items.caution: Official investigation/finding signal; mechanism-specific R/A/E domains require separate data, image, authorship, or peer-review labels.
items.semantic_rationale: Official investigations/findings of misconduct inherently question research content reliability, may involve authorship or disclosure issues, can relate to editorial/peer review governance if misconduct affected review, and always trigger post-publication oversight processes. The definition explicitly mentions institutional and government actors, and the process is an official misconduct investigation.

items.definition_used: Statement by journal, publisher, company, institution, government agency or author that one or more authors committed misconduct.
items.caution: Broad misconduct-process metadata; do not infer content, attribution, editorial mechanism, or actor responsibility unless a mechanism-specific co-label is present. Contextual-exclusion sensitivity is required.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition indicates a statement of author misconduct, which can affect research content reliability, authorship integrity, editorial governance, and post-publication oversight, as misconduct may involve data fabrication, authorship fraud, peer review manipulation, or failure to disclose conflicts. The process signal is official misconduct process, and actor contexts include those making the statement.

items.definition_used: Statement by journal, publisher, company, institution, government agency or author that one or more companies/institutions committed misconduct.
items.caution: Broad misconduct-process metadata; do not infer content, attribution, editorial mechanism, or actor responsibility unless a mechanism-specific co-label is present. Contextual-exclusion sensitivity is required.
items.semantic_rationale: Misconduct by a company/institution can affect research content reliability, authorship/disclosure integrity, editorial/peer review governance, and post-publication oversight. The definition indicates an investigation by or statement from an entity, making institutional investigation the process signal, with the company/institution as the actor context. The problem object is set to article_general due to lack of specificity.

items.definition_used: Statement by journal, publisher, company, institution, government agency or author that one or more third party(ies) committed misconduct.
items.caution: Broad misconduct-process metadata; do not infer content, attribution, editorial mechanism, or actor responsibility unless a mechanism-specific co-label is present. Contextual-exclusion sensitivity is required.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition states that a third party committed misconduct, which can affect research content reliability, authorship/attribution integrity, editorial/peer review governance, and post-publication oversight. The process signal is third-party investigation, and the actor context is third party. Problem object is set to article_general as the misconduct could involve any aspect of the article.

items.definition_used: The journal or publisher has stated that no further action will be taken.
items.caution: This is a status notice about the conclusion of an investigation, not a direct indicator of manuscript content issues. It may appear alongside other reasons that provide more specific context.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a journal/publisher statement that no further action will be taken, which relates to post-publication transparency and due process oversight, but does not directly indicate issues with research content, authorship, or editorial governance.

items.raw_reason: Nonpayment of Fees and/or Refusal to Pay
items.canonical_reason: Nonpayment of Fees and/or Refusal to Pay
items.definition_used: Fees for services, licenses or access were not paid and/or completed, and/or there was a refusal to pay fees.
items.caution: The reason describes a financial transaction failure, not a manuscript integrity issue. It does not directly map to any of the four manuscript-facing categories, which focus on research content, authorship, peer review, or post-publication oversight.
items.semantic_rationale: Nonpayment of fees is a business/administrative matter, not a content, authorship, peer review, or post-publication oversight issue per the supplied definitions.

items.definition_used: The paper/abstract/poster was not presented at the conference for which it was accepted.
items.caution: The reason describes a conference presentation status, not a manuscript integrity issue. It does not directly map to any of the four manuscript-facing categories, which focus on research content, attribution, editorial governance, or post-publication oversight.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition indicates that the work was not presented as planned, which is a procedural or policy matter (publication_policy_or_sanction) concerning the article's general status, but it does not inherently imply unreliability of research content, authorship/attribution problems, editorial/peer review issues, or post-publication transparency failures.

items.definition_used: No notice was published by the journal or publisher.
items.caution: This is a status-only label indicating absence of a notice, not a substantive reason for retraction. It does not imply any underlying cause or fault.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a lack of published notice by the journal or publisher, which directly maps to post-publication transparency and notice opacity.

items.definition_used: A notice provides minimal information as to the cause of the notice, or the original item is watermaked as retracted or corrected without explanation
items.caution: This is a metadata/status label indicating opacity of the notice itself, not a substantive reason for retraction. It does not directly implicate research content, authorship, or editorial processes, but it relates to post-publication transparency.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a notice that lacks substantive explanation, which directly maps to post-publication transparency and due process oversight. The problem object is the availability/notice status, and the process signal is notice opacity. The actor context is journal/publisher as the source of the opaque notice.

items.raw_reason: Notice - Unable to Access via current resources
items.canonical_reason: Notice – Unable to Access via current resources
items.definition_used: The notice is paywalled by the journal/publisher, only available in print or is in some form unavailable for inspection.
items.caution: This is a metadata/status label about notice accessibility, not a substantive integrity issue. It does not imply any problem with the research content, authorship, or editorial processes.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a notice that is inaccessible due to paywall or format, which directly relates to post-publication transparency and due process oversight, as it hinders the ability to inspect the notice. No other manuscript categories are supported.

items.definition_used: One or more authors objected to the notice or the wording of the notice.
items.caution: This reason indicates author disagreement with a notice, which is a post-publication transparency signal, not a direct indicator of manuscript content or process flaws. It does not confirm any underlying problem with the research, authorship, or editorial processes.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes author objections to a notice or its wording, which directly relates to post-publication transparency and due process oversight. It does not inherently imply issues with research content, attribution, or editorial governance, so only the post-publication category is assigned.

items.definition_used: One or more companies/institutions objected to the notice or the wording of the notice.
items.caution: The reason describes an objection to the notice itself, not necessarily a problem with the underlying research content. It is a metadata transparency signal about post-publication communication, not a direct indicator of manuscript integrity issues.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition focuses on objections to the notice or its wording, which relates to post-publication transparency and due process oversight. It does not directly address research content reliability, authorship/attribution integrity, or editorial/peer review governance. The problem object is the notice status, and the process signal is notice opacity, with company/institution as the actor context.

items.definition_used: One or more third parties objected to the notice or the wording of the notice.
items.caution: The reason describes a post-publication objection to a notice, which is a transparency/due-process signal, not a direct indicator of manuscript content or authorship issues. It is status-oriented and does not inherently imply research unreliability or misconduct.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition centers on third-party objections to a notice, which falls under post-publication transparency and due process oversight, as it concerns the handling and wording of retraction or correction notices.

items.raw_reason: Original Data and/or Images not Provided and/or not Available
items.canonical_reason: Original Data and/or Images not Provided and/or not Available
items.definition_used: The original data or images for the published study is no longer available or is not given to the editorial staff.
items.caution: The reason indicates unavailability of data/images, which impacts research content reliability and transparency, but does not specify cause or fault.
items.semantic_rationale: Unavailability of original data/images directly undermines verification of research content (research_content_reliability) and reflects a post-publication transparency failure (post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight).

items.definition_used: When a journal/publisher/institution states that a paper came from a paper mill or the paper is in a list of paper mill papers. RW may also use this reason to reflect that RW has identified multiple paper mill criteria applying to this paper.
items.caution: Paper mill designation is a strong integrity signal but does not specify exact content flaws; it implies systemic fabrication and compromised processes.
items.semantic_rationale: Paper mill indicates fabricated or manipulated content (research_content_reliability), fraudulent authorship/attribution (attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity), and subverted peer review (editorial_peer_review_governance).

items.definition_used: Plagiarism of any of the data.
items.semantic_rationale: Plagiarism of data directly compromises the originality and reliability of research content, and constitutes a failure in attribution and authorship integrity.

items.definition_used: Plagiarism of one or more images.
items.semantic_rationale: Image plagiarism directly undermines research content reliability by duplicating visual data without proper attribution, and violates attribution/authorship integrity by misrepresenting the origin of the image.

items.definition_used: Plagiarism of any of the text.
items.semantic_rationale: Plagiarism of text directly violates attribution and authorship integrity, as it involves misappropriation of written content without proper credit.

items.definition_used: Plagiarism of a published item, or undefined sections of it.
items.semantic_rationale: Plagiarism directly violates attribution and authorship integrity, and undermines research content reliability by misrepresenting originality. The definition explicitly involves reuse of published material without proper credit.

items.definition_used: When a journal/publisher states that no manuscripts will be accepted from one or more authors of the original article. Bans could be for a limited time or indefinitely.
items.caution: Publishing ban is a post-publication sanction, not a direct indicator of manuscript content or process flaws. It reflects journal policy enforcement, not necessarily a retraction cause.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a journal/publisher-imposed ban on future submissions from authors, which is a post-publication oversight action (publication_policy_or_sanction) involving journal/publisher and author actors. It fits post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight as a transparency/due-process measure, but does not directly indicate issues with research content, authorship, or editorial processes.

items.definition_used: The original article is removed from access on the journal’s website or publishing platform.
items.caution: This is a status-only term indicating removal of access, not the underlying cause. It does not directly assert problems with research content, authorship, or editorial processes, but it relates to post-publication transparency.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes removal of the article from the journal's platform, which is a post-publication action affecting transparency and access. It maps to post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight because it concerns the availability and oversight of the published record, but it is a broad status signal rather than a direct indication of content or process flaws.

items.definition_used: When repetition(s) of experiment(s), using the same materials and methods, failed to replicate the results in the original article.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition directly addresses failure to replicate results, which undermines the reliability of the research content. This maps strictly to research_content_reliability.

items.definition_used: The change of an item’s status reflecting that a retracted item will be replaced with a new publication in the same journal. The journal has indicated that the replacement should be cited as the version of record.
items.caution: This is a status/notice term describing a publication-status change (retraction with replacement), not a root cause. It signals post-publication correction/update process but does not directly indicate a problem with research content, authorship, or editorial governance. Main figure prevalence is not recommended because the label is primarily about metadata transparency and version-of-record replacement.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a change in publication status where a retracted item is replaced by a new version of record. This directly relates to post-publication transparency and due process oversight (manuscript category) because it involves a formal correction/update process (process_signal) managed by the journal/publisher (actor_context). The problem object is the article as a whole, as the replacement affects the entire publication.

items.definition_used: Used when an editor’s credentials are false/forged or when an editor subverts one or more processes under their purview. An “editor” may be an established editor affiliated with the journal or a guest editor.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes an editor subverting processes under their purview, which directly maps to editorial/peer review governance failures. The actor is explicitly the editor, and the process signal is editorial breach with potential peer review compromise.

items.definition_used: An intentional action by a third party, without the researchers’ knowledge or consent, to sabotage or contaminate experimental ingredients or processes in order to influence experimental outcome(s).
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes intentional contamination of experimental materials by a third party, directly compromising the reliability of research content. The process signal is third-party investigation as the sabotage is an external action investigated by the affected researchers or institution.

items.definition_used: The publication of several articles using the same dataset by breaking it into sections, with the intent of exploiting a limited data set for the production of several published works. This does not apply to large multi-group studies such as the Framingham Heart Study.
items.caution: Content partitioning and publication-integrity signal; editorial/peer-review process assignment requires a separate editorial or peer-review reason label.
items.semantic_rationale: Salami slicing fragments a dataset into multiple publications, undermining the reliability of reported results by creating non-independent evidence. It also involves inadequate disclosure of data overlap, breaching attribution and transparency norms. Editorial processes may fail to identify such fragmentation, implicating peer review governance. Thus, research_content_reliability, attribution_authorship_disclosure_integrity, and editorial_peer_review_governance are all supported.

items.definition_used: The duplicated or plagiarized content was taken from an academic dissertation or thesis.
items.caution: None
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes duplicated or plagiarized content from a dissertation/thesis, which directly implicates attribution/authorship integrity and raises concerns about the reliability of the research content due to potential plagiarism.

items.definition_used: The duplicated or plagiarized content was taken during the peer review process.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes content taken during peer review, indicating a breach of peer review confidentiality and potential plagiarism, which directly impacts attribution integrity and editorial governance.

items.definition_used: The duplicated or plagiarized content was created via a translation from one language to another.
items.caution: Translation-based duplication implies plagiarism, which is an authorship/attribution integrity issue, and may also affect content reliability if the translated content is presented as original research.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes duplicated or plagiarized content created via translation, directly implicating attribution and authorship integrity, and potentially undermining research content reliability if the translated material is misrepresented.

items.definition_used: The original article is removed from the journal’s publishing platform and the notice states the removal will be for an undefined period of time.
items.caution: This is a status/notice term describing a temporary removal with undefined duration. It does not directly indicate a problem with research content, authorship, or editorial governance, but it relates to post-publication transparency and due process oversight because the removal and opaque notice affect access and clarity.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a temporary removal of an article with an undefined period, which is a post-publication action affecting availability and transparency. It fits post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight because it involves a notice about removal status and opaque timeline, but it is not a substantive content or process issue. Main figure not recommended as it is a status-only label.

items.definition_used: A change in the copyright and/or ownership of the article or any of its content.
items.caution: The definition describes a legal status change, not a direct integrity problem with research content, authorship, peer review, or post-publication oversight. It does not map to any of the four manuscript-facing categories.
items.semantic_rationale: The reason concerns a change in copyright/ownership, which is a legal rights matter. It does not inherently indicate issues with research reliability, attribution integrity, editorial governance, or post-publication transparency processes as defined.

items.definition_used: Any of the data is unreliable.
items.caution: The definition is broad and does not specify cause, investigation, or actor. It directly indicates a problem with data reliability, which falls under research content reliability. No other categories are clearly supported.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition states that any data is unreliable, which directly concerns the trustworthiness of research content, fitting the research_content_reliability category.

items.definition_used: One or more images, or part(s) of one or more images, are unreliable.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition directly states that images are unreliable, which undermines the trustworthiness of research content, fitting research_content_reliability. No other categories are supported.

items.definition_used: Any of the results and/or conclusions are unreliable.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition directly states that results and/or conclusions are unreliable, which maps to research_content_reliability. No process or actor is specified, so actor_context is unclear.

items.definition_used: The article has a correction after this notice.
items.caution: This is a metadata/status label indicating a correction exists, not a substantive integrity issue. It does not directly imply problems with research content, authorship, or peer review.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a post-publication update to a correction, which falls under post-publication transparency and due process oversight. It does not inherently indicate issues with research content reliability, attribution/authorship, or editorial/peer review governance.

items.definition_used: The article has an expression of concern after this notice.
items.caution: This is a status/notice term indicating that an Expression of Concern has been added. It does not specify the underlying reason for the concern, so it cannot be assigned to content, authorship, or peer review categories without further information.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a post-publication notice (Expression of Concern) added to the article, which falls under post-publication transparency and due process oversight. The problem object is the article as a whole, and the process signal is notice opacity because the notice itself does not reveal the specific issue. The actor context is journal/publisher as the entity issuing the notice.

items.definition_used: The article has a retraction after this notice.
items.caution: This is a metadata/status label indicating a notice update, not a substantive reason for retraction. It does not directly implicate research content, authorship, or editorial processes.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a notice status change (retraction after this notice), which falls under post-publication transparency and due process oversight as it pertains to the metadata record and availability of the article. It does not inherently indicate issues with research content, authorship, or editorial governance.

items.definition_used: At least one prior notice for the article has been upgraded or updated with this notice.
items.caution: This reason is a metadata status indicator about notice progression, not a direct content or process issue. It signals that a prior notice was upgraded/updated, which relates to post-publication transparency but does not itself indicate a specific problem with research content, authorship, or editorial governance. Main figure recommendation is false because the reason is status-only and does not substantiate a primary manuscript category for prevalence analysis.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a change in notice status (upgrade/update of a prior notice), which directly pertains to post-publication transparency and due process oversight. It does not inherently imply issues with research content, authorship, or editorial peer review, but rather reflects the evolution of public notices about the article.

items.definition_used: The article has been retracted as part of a journal’s process of keeping guidelines or reviews current for professional use.
items.caution: This is a status-only notice about a journal's routine update process, not a finding of unreliability or misconduct. It does not imply any problem with the original content.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a journal-driven process to keep guidelines or reviews current, which is a post-publication administrative action. This aligns with post_publication_transparency_due_process_oversight as it involves a publication status change for transparency, but it does not indicate issues with research content, authorship, or editorial governance. The problem object is article_general because the entire article is withdrawn, and process signals include publication_policy_or_sanction and notice_opacity due to the withdrawal notice. Actor context is journal_publisher as the initiating entity.

items.raw_reason: Withdrawn to Publish in Different Journal
items.canonical_reason: Withdrawn to Publish in Different Journal
items.definition_used: The article was taken from one journal/platform or access type to be published in a different journal/platform or with a different access type.
items.caution: This is a status/notice term describing a withdrawal for republication elsewhere. It does not directly indicate a problem with research content, authorship, or peer review integrity, but it relates to editorial governance and post-publication transparency. Main figure not recommended because the reason is primarily a publication-process metadata signal rather than a substantive integrity issue.
items.semantic_rationale: The definition describes a withdrawal to republish in a different journal or platform, which involves editorial governance (handling of manuscript transfers) and post-publication transparency (notice of withdrawal). It does not inherently imply unreliability of research content or authorship/attribution issues.

post_codex_global_rules: Retraction Watch Reason terms remain non-exclusive curated metadata signals, not fault, liability, cause, or responsibility determinations.
The four R/A/E/P domains are analyst-defined metadata signal domains for descriptive stratification.
Investigation-by-X labels identify investigation source/locus, not actor fault, oversight failure, or substantive cause.
Generic Misconduct-by-X and Miscommunication labels remain principal P-only in the main analysis for continuity but require contextual-exclusion sensitivity reporting.
Notice/status labels can retain semantic P mapping but remain contextual/not principal; No assigned primary domain means no principal R/A/E/P assignment, not absence of Retraction Watch metadata.
Object type governs plagiarism/duplication rules: text-only attribution, data/image evidence reliability, article-level R+A when appropriate.

final_manuscript_category_labels.attribution_authorship_disclosure_integr: Attribution, authorship, disclosure and ethics integrity

final_manuscript_category_explanations.research_content_reliability: Signals that the reliability, reproducibility, validity, or evidentiary integrity of the research content itself is questioned. Includes data, image, methods/materials, analyses, results/conclusions, non-reproducibility, paper-mill and AI/computer-generated content signals when the official definition concerns article-content reliability.
final_manuscript_category_explanations.attribution_authorship_disclosure_integr: Signals concerning authorship, affiliation, consent/approval to publish, plagiarism, duplicate publication, citation/reference/attribution, copyright/ownership, conflicts of interest, or research-ethics disclosure/approval. This is an integrity/relationship-transparency family, not a blame category.
final_manuscript_category_explanations.editorial_peer_review_governance: Signals concerning peer-review integrity, editorial decision-making, rogue/editorial breach, journal/publisher error, or governance of the pre-publication editorial process. Investigation-by-journal/publisher alone is not treated as editorial fault.
final_manuscript_category_explanations.post_publication_transparency_due_proces: Signals concerning investigation source, official/institutional/third-party oversight, notice transparency, communication, objection, correction/retraction status, removal/availability, or legal/ORI/misconduct process. This category means post-publication process/oversight metadata, not due-process failure or fault by the named actor.

main_figure_rule: Use maincat_* flags generated only from reason items with main_figure_recommended=true. cat_* flags preserve broader semantic/audit category assignments.
